stories.headline: Vatican City: Pope Leo back at his window, easing back into his duties
stories.body: Less than a day after leaving Gemelli hospital, Pope Leo XIV prayed Sunday’s Angelus from the Apostolic Palace window as thousands cheered on a cloudy St. Peter’s Square. “I have truly sensed your support,” he said, thanking the doctors, nurses and staff, adding that the illness had made him feel close to everyone living with sickness and that, having “overcome this delicate phase,” he will “gradually resume” his activities. Reflecting on “Render unto Caesar,” he said it means being truthful and free of servile fear or hypocrisy, free to do good. His surgeon, Prof. Stefano Margaritora, says there is no clinical reason he cannot make the Nov. 6–17 journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

stories.headline: Vatican City: Pope names a new International Theological Commission
stories.body: This morning’s bulletin named 24 members to the International Theological Commission, the panel of theologians that advises the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith. They include Fr. Khaled Anatolios of Notre Dame and Prof. Boyd Taylor Coolman of Boston College, scholars from India, Malaysia, Kenya, Benin, Mexico, Argentina and Brazil, and six women, among them Sara Parvis of Edinburgh and Anne-Sophie Vivier-Muresan, dean of theology at the Institut Catholique de Paris. It is one of the first big personnel signals since the Pope’s surgery that the Curia’s work is moving again.

stories.headline: Africa: Drones push Eritrean troops back in Tigray; Adigrat on edge
stories.body: Residents of Adigrat, about 40 kilometers from the Eritrean border, describe burnt-out trucks in the streets after federal drone strikes on Eritrean soldiers, schools shut for days, shortages in the shops, and one resident says policing has collapsed, with robberies and stabbings. Some Eritrean troops have gone home while others remain near the frontier, and the border town of Zalambessa stays tense; Eritrea denies its troops entered at all. The pro-government Tigray Peace Force says core TPLF fighters crossed into Eritrea and is offering the rest a grace period, while Tigrayan forces claim gains near Mekelle that no one has verified. Addis Ababa has named a six-month transitional administration, and the Frontlines.et tracker independently verified 3 of 7 reports on Sunday.

stories.headline: Africa: Kabila leads Congo’s rebels as Ebola reaches an eighth province
stories.body: Former President Joseph Kabila now heads the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, a new coalition announced in Goma that replaces the AFC–M23 alliance and calls for resistance against President Félix Tshisekedi “by all means”; Kinshasa accuses him of planning a general attack, and a military court sentenced him to death in absentia last year. The front says it will honor the commitments made in the Qatar-brokered Doha talks, though fighting continues in North and South Kivu. Meanwhile the Bundibugyo-strain Ebola outbreak has spread to Nord-Ubangi, with two cases and one death in Wapinda, the eighth province hit; a tracker of official reports counts 9,415 confirmed cases and 4,536 deaths as of Oct. 16.

stories.headline: Africa: Sudan’s drone war reaches the east as Darfur strikes continue
stories.body: The army says its air defenses brought down RSF drones aimed at Gedaref, Kassala and dam infrastructure in the east without major damage, while it keeps striking what it calls RSF command centers in Nyala. The RSF says one of those strikes hit a livestock market, and Dabanga reports drone strikes killing civilians in West Darfur and Kordofan; neither side’s tallies have been independently confirmed. The east had been the government’s safe rear, so drones reaching Kassala and the dams widen the war’s map.

stories.headline: Asia: Iran claims a third tanker hit a mine; says Hormuz is ‘closed’
stories.body: Late Sunday Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said another tanker struck a mine in the southern Strait of Hormuz, the blast hitting its engine room, after two supertankers carrying about 2 million barrels each were reported hit Saturday; no ship has been named and none of the claims is independently confirmed. The Guards say ships running with tracking switched off and using “unauthorized” routes will face a firm response. U.S. Central Command says 400 ships moved through last week, while Kpler counts flows at about 68% of the pre-war level, and Brent touched $110 on Friday.

stories.headline: Asia: Trump endorses Netanyahu; Yemen’s forces push on Bab al-Mandeb
stories.body: President Trump endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, calling him “a Great Warrior Prime Minister,” a backing he had withheld for months, ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 election, the first since the Hamas attack of 2023. In Yemen, Saudi-backed government forces opened a new push to clear Houthi fighters from the hills, trenches and minefields above the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and the Houthis answered with first-person-view kamikaze drones. Both fronts feed the same oil story as Hormuz: the Red Sea and the Gulf are now contested at once.

stories.headline: Asia: China’s growth beats forecasts at 4.5%; Takaichi sends Yasukuni offering
stories.body: Overnight Beijing said its economy grew 4.5% in July–September from a year earlier, up from 4.3% and better than expected, powered by exports while consumers stay cautious; that is the bottom of its 4.5–5% target. In Tokyo, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sent a personally paid offering, not a visit, to Yasukuni Shrine for its autumn festival while her land minister went in person, a gesture China and Korea read as honoring Japan’s militarist past. Japan also marked 70 years since the 1956 declaration with Moscow and vowed to keep seeking a deal on the islands off Hokkaido.

stories.headline: Europe: Russia fires 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv; 550,000 homes lose power
stories.body: Overnight Russia sent 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and its region in several waves, plus cruise missiles and 269 Shahed drones, of which Ukraine says it downed 243, hitting 25 locations and more than 10 energy facilities. A 21-year-old woman was killed in Kyiv, where a clinic, a fitness club and the left-bank Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations were hit, and another woman died in Irpin, with three children among the injured there. Zelenskyy said there was “no early warning from our partners”; Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in Uzbekistan, said there has been no pause in intelligence sharing. Moscow says it hit a data center and drone and missile storage.

stories.headline: Europe: Ukraine’s 1,000-drone raid sets St. Petersburg oil sites ablaze
stories.body: On Sunday Ukraine launched one of its largest drone attacks of the war; Russia says it downed 1,015 drones over 15 regions, Crimea and the Black Sea. In St. Petersburg the oil terminal and the Ruchi depot caught fire, one person was killed and five hurt, the airport restricted flights, and about 20,000 people in the Leningrad region lost power. President Trump criticized Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil and defended pausing new sanctions so as not to “foolishly” drive Moscow from the table; Zelenskyy told NBC that siding with Moscow would be a “historic mistake.”

stories.headline: Europe: France counts 2,400 arrests; Macron decries ‘unbridled violence’
stories.body: Saturday’s cost-of-living and school protests were mostly peaceful, but separate rioting and looting left about 2,400 people arrested, a record 855 in Paris, nearly 1,000 police and gendarmes hurt, more than 1,500 shops ransacked, and Limoges’s 19th-century town hall burned; clashes flared again Sunday at Place de la République. In a televised address Macron asked “how could French people do this to France?”, blamed ultra-left groups and criminals, and allowed prefects to ban gatherings. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered to resign and Macron refused, ordering a review of the intelligence failures; protests also spread to Spain, Italy and Portugal.

stories.headline: Ukraine, deeper: a week of ‘energy ceasefire’ that never held
stories.body: Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on Oct. 11 without details; Zelenskyy says Russia has since hit Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sites 76 times, and that last week alone brought almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 glide bombs and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic. Kyiv, which paused its own strikes on Russian energy for a few days, has now answered with the St. Petersburg raid, and winter heating is the stake for both sides. On the diplomatic track, Zelenskyy spoke Sunday with envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the Oct. 9 talks in Miami and “next steps,” and the Pope’s Friday plea for a humanitarian truce in occupied Oleshky, where about 2,000 people are trapped, is still waiting for any sign of aid getting through.

stories.headline: North America: Alberta votes today on starting a path to separation
stories.body: Polls are open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Mountain time (11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Eastern) on a 10-question referendum, one of which asks whether Alberta should stay in Canada or begin a legal process toward a future, binding separation vote. About a million people voted early; the last Abacus poll had remain at 68%. Unofficial results come tonight and official ones Oct. 29, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has asked for a decisive answer.

stories.headline: North America: Grass fire kills four Canadian soldiers in live-fire training
stories.body: A grass fire swept through a live-ammunition training area at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alberta, on Saturday, killing four service members and injuring 39 others, 19 critically. Officials thought it was contained enough to keep training, but the wind shifted and the flames were on the soldiers in under a minute. Carney called it one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military at home and ordered flags lowered nationwide.

stories.headline: South America: Brazil’s first runoff debate ends in accusations and chaos
stories.body: In Sunday night’s two-hour Band debate, President Lula dared Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro to open his and his family’s bank and phone records; Flávio refused and joked that Lula doesn’t even carry a cellphone. They clashed over corruption, crime and ties to Washington, with Flávio pitching troops on borders and ports and a million AI cameras, and analysts said little reached undecided voters. Supporters in the studio broke into a tumult during closing statements, and the runoff is Sunday, Oct. 25; Flávio led the first round 47% to 45%.

stories.headline: Oceania: Guam restores power after super typhoon Champi’s near miss
stories.body: Champi passed about 10 miles south of Guam as a super typhoon, and forecasters say a direct landfall would have been devastating. By Monday morning local time, 90% of transmission lines and all 30 critical substations were back, 70% of distribution circuits were energized, and about 650 water customers in southern and central villages still had no pressure, with tankers deployed. Trash pickup resumed and a green-waste site opens Wednesday.

stories.headline: Ending the war: Trump defends the sanctions pause as diplomacy
stories.body: Promise: end the Russia–Ukraine war quickly. What was done: on Sunday Trump defended Friday’s hold on the Graham Act’s new tariffs and sanctions, saying he would not “foolishly” drive Moscow from the bargaining table, and his envoys Witkoff and Kushner briefed Zelenskyy on next steps. Impact so far: Zelenskyy says Russia hit Ukraine’s energy sites 76 times in the week after the announced energy truce, and overnight it fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv. Supporters say pressure without talks prolongs the war; critics, including Hakeem Jeffries, say relief without reciprocity rewards Putin.

stories.headline: Lowering prices: a mixed scorecard two weeks before the midterms
stories.body: Promise: cheaper groceries, gas under $2, 2% mortgages. The data CBS News compiled: gas averaged $4.37 on Oct. 9, up 47% since the Iran war began; groceries are up 4% since November 2024; the 30-year mortgage is 7.28%. Where it moved the right way: prescription drug prices are down 3.9% from their February 2025 peak, which the White House credits to its “most favored nation” pricing, and car insurance is down 5.5% since February. The White House points to the tax cuts and nearly 20 trade deals; economists cite tariffs and the war as the biggest drags.

stories.headline: MAHA: Kennedy tours rural EMS and health-workforce programs
stories.body: Promise: rebuild health care for rural and working Americans. What was done: in Concord, N.H., Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. showcased a rural EMS program funded by the federal Rural Health Transformation Program, then toured a health-professions training center in Virginia Beach on workforce shortages. Impact: more trained responders in places that lack them. He also again questioned the hepatitis B vaccine’s pre-licensing trials, a claim that University of Minnesota researchers say is wrong, pointing to a 1980 placebo-controlled study.

What was done, per preliminary DHS data from Friday: 98,708 southwest-border apprehensions in fiscal 2026, about 95% below Biden-era peaks, total nationwide encounters of 379,243, the lowest in agency history, and zero Border Patrol releases. stories.body: SpaceX, now public as SPCX, posts third-quarter results Tuesday with an audio webcast at 4:30 p.m. Eastern; analysts expect 18 cents a share on about $13.16 billion in revenue, with Starlink growth and its AI arm in focus. Tesla follows Wednesday after the close, call at 5:30 p.m.; consensus is about 45 cents a share on $28.1 billion, and LSEG sees earnings down 14.5% from a year ago even though deliveries of 486,532 beat estimates. stories.headline: SPHEREx finds water and methane on lonely brown dwarfs
stories.body: NASA’s SPHEREx sky-mapper measured 37 nearby brown dwarfs, objects too small to become stars, in 102 colors and found water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane, from scorching ones near 4,000°F to the coldest known, colder than a freezer, about 7 light-years away. Five leading atmosphere models got the broad chemistry right but stumbled where clouds start clearing; the team has thousands more to analyze, and the data are free to the public.

stories.headline: Miami: Wenski presses ‘no human being is a problem’ on executions and mental illness
stories.body: With Florida carrying out 16 executions this year, more than half the national total, Archbishop Thomas Wenski is urging Catholics to look past political “tribes” and see the convicted as still made in God’s image, backing the Florida bishops’ July pastoral letter against the death penalty. He also told a NAMI conference that a person in a mental-health crisis too often ends up in jail rather than care: “We are a people of both,” prayer and psychiatry. stories.headline: Countdown to the Kingdom: checked this morning, latest posts dated Oct. 16
stories.body: Checked Monday morning: the newest items on Countdown to the Kingdom are still four posts dated Oct. 16, Mark Mallett’s “What Is the Promised Peace?”, messages attributed to Our Lady through Angela and Simona of Zaro di Ischia, Italy, and through Pedro Regis of Anguera, Brazil. Going deeper into Mallett’s theme: the site frames it around the century-old promise, from Fatima onward, of a “Triumph of the Immaculate Heart” that ushers in a “period of peace,” and asks what that peace is and how it comes. Zaro’s seers receive messages on the 8th and 26th of each month, so the next are expected Oct. 26; the site itself reminds readers that only the Church judges authenticity and that none of this binds like public revelation.

stories.headline: Ending the war and lowering fuel costs: the Graham Act waiver
stories.body: Promise: Trump pledged to end the Russia–Ukraine war quickly and to bring down energy prices. What was done: Friday’s order suspended the Graham Act’s 500% tariff on Russian goods, the 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, and most new sanctions, after an earlier waiver let Russian diesel flow through April 2027; existing sanctions stay. The case for it: keeping Russian fuel in world markets during the Iran war restrains prices before the midterms, avoids tariff fights with China and India, and keeps an economic channel open with Moscow. The case against: Congress passed the law and the president signed it only on Sept. 18, Moscow’s envoy hailed the move, and Kyiv says it rewards Russia on the very night of one of the largest strikes on Ukraine’s grid. stories.headline: Roman Space Telescope is nearly 30% sharper than required
stories.body: After weeks of checkout, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched Aug. 30, measured optical error of just 63 nanometers against a 90-nanometer requirement, so its Wide Field Instrument will deliver image quality nearly 30% better than predicted. Engineers moved the secondary mirror about one-sixteenth the width of a human hair, which they compare to stacking a single penny on the tip of the Empire State Building. stories.headline: Ending the war and lowering fuel costs: the Graham Act waiver
stories.body: Promise: Trump pledged to end the Russia–Ukraine war quickly and to bring down energy prices. What was done: Friday’s order suspended the Graham Act’s 500% tariff on Russian goods, the 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, and most new sanctions, after an earlier waiver let Russian diesel flow through April 2027; existing sanctions stay. The case for it: keeping Russian fuel in world markets during the Iran war restrains prices before the midterms, avoids tariff fights with China and India, and keeps an economic channel open with Moscow. The case against: Congress passed the law and the president signed it only on Sept. 18, Moscow’s envoy hailed the move, and Kyiv says it rewards Russia on the very night of one of the largest strikes on Ukraine’s grid. Verdict: the energy-price aim is being pursued; the war is not ending.

stories.headline: Vatican City: Pope says Mass for Gemelli staff; Sunday Angelus confirmed
stories.body: On his fourth day in hospital, Pope Leo XIV celebrated noon Mass in the room set up on Gemelli’s 10th floor, gave Communion to off-duty doctors, nurses, and Vatican gendarmes, and thanked them in his homily for caring for patients “in their frailty” — and for him. The Vatican released the first photos since Tuesday’s lung surgery: the Pope standing at a small altar in green vestments. Friday’s bulletin from Dr. Luigi Carbone and Prof. Stefano Margaritora says blood tests and a chest X-ray confirm “steady improvement,” and that he carries out daily activities with complete autonomy. The Press Office says Sunday’s Angelus “will take place,” though not yet whether from the hospital or the Vatican; discharge is still expected around Tuesday, Oct. 20.
stories.why: First pictures and a public prayer on Sunday are the clearest signs yet that the recovery is on track.

Critical Threats analysts read the display as groundwork to justify strikes inside Eritrea on self-defense grounds, while the U.S., EU, U.K., and Canada urge restraint; in Amhara, Fano rebels keep taking rural towns in South Wollo and North Shewa.

beats.headline: Vance’s fraud pledge spreads; peptide plan’s fine print; tax relief recap.

stories.headline: War on fraud: Vance pledge gathers signers; results are self-reported
stories.body: Promise: Trump promised to root out waste, fraud, and abuse in federal programs. What was done: Vice President Vance, who heads the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, asked officials at every level to sign a pledge to stop fraud “before the money goes out,” keep benefits for eligible Americans, and prosecute fraudsters; the White House lists Cabinet members, more than a dozen governors, state attorneys general, and dozens of members of Congress. Impact claimed: Labor says it has uncovered $22 billion in labor fraud, Education says it has prevented more than $2 billion in student-aid fraud, and the FBI cites six “Most Wanted” fraud arrests tied to over $2 billion. Room for disagreement: a pledge is a statement of intent, not a law; the figures are the agencies’ own, not independently audited; and every elected signer listed is a Republican — Rep. Rudy Yakym asked why no Democrat has signed. In progress.

sources.name: White House: Coalition in the war on fraud

stories.headline: MAHA peptides, deeper: advisers overruled staff; telehealth firms wait
stories.body: Promise: Kennedy said the FDA’s “war” on peptides would end. What was done: HHS sent the White House an “interim access policy” that would use enforcement discretion, telling compounding pharmacies they won’t be targeted for making peptides like BPC-157; formally listing them as safe to compound would take rulemaking that could last years. In July a panel of outside advisers, chosen by HHS and including people who work in the peptide field, recommended lifting limits on six of seven peptides, against the conclusion of FDA staff scientists. Impact: Hims & Hers and Noom plan to sell peptides if access eases, in a market analysts put at $2 billion to $3 billion; supporters call it medical freedom, and the FDA has listed risks including contamination, allergic reactions, and tumor growth. Not yet in effect.

stories.headline: No tax on tips and overtime: partly kept, capped through 2028
stories.body: Promise: Trump campaigned on ending federal taxes on tips and overtime. What was done: The July 2025 tax law created deductions, not a full repeal: up to $25,000 of tips, plus the extra “half” of time-and-a-half overtime, through 2028, with payroll taxes still owed. Treasury’s first-season data: more than 7.5 million filers claimed the tips deduction (average above $7,000) and more than 29 million the overtime deduction (average above $3,100), mostly households under $100,000. Impact: Independent Tax Policy Center estimates put the average saving at about $1,480 for the roughly 3% of taxpayers who get the tips break and about $1,200 for the 10% who get the overtime break. Kept in part: real relief for those who qualify, but it is temporary, and the bill also cut Medicaid and SNAP.

Musk set production for 2028 but gave no price. There are three trims: Performance (two seats, 0–60 under 1.6 seconds, $50,000 to reserve), Thrust (rear thrusters, under 0.9 seconds, $250,000 to reserve), and an invite-only, single-seat Rocket with a “full flight system” that isn’t street-legal. Tesla claims range over 300 miles (less than half the 620 promised in 2017) and top speed over 230 mph. Analysts see a low-volume halo car, and some read the event as marketing for a Tesla–SpaceX merger.

stories.body: Administrator Jared Isaacman named Stephen Cash director of Marshall in Huntsville, effective Monday, Oct. 19, calling him “a Marshall legend.” A four-decade veteran who once managed the shuttle propulsion program, Cash returns to the center where his career began; Rae Ann Meyer, who led the center during the transition, continues to serve. stories.headline: No tax on tips and overtime: partly kept, capped through 2028
stories.body: Promise: Trump campaigned on ending federal taxes on tips and overtime. What was done: The July 2025 tax law created deductions, not a full repeal: up to $25,000 of tips, plus the extra “half” of time-and-a-half overtime, through 2028, with payroll taxes still owed. Treasury’s first-season data: more than 7.5 million filers claimed the tips deduction (average above $7,000) and more than 29 million the overtime deduction (average above $3,100), mostly households under $100,000. Impact: Independent Tax Policy Center estimates put the average saving at about $1,480 for the roughly 3% of taxpayers who get the tips break and about $1,200 for the 10% who get the overtime break. Kept in part: real relief for those who qualify, but it is temporary, and the bill also cut Medicaid and SNAP.

stories.headline: MAHA peptides plan reaches the White House, not yet in effect
stories.body: Promise: Before taking office, Kennedy said the FDA’s crackdown on peptides and other wellness products would end. What was done: On Thursday HHS sent the White House a peptide “interim access policy.” People familiar with it say it would let compounding pharmacies temporarily make popular peptides like BPC-157 without FDA enforcement. Impact: Supporters call it medical freedom and a safer alternative to gray-market imports from China. FDA staff scientists say none of these peptides has been studied enough to show it is safe or works; risks include contamination, allergic reactions, and tumor growth. In progress, not yet in effect.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City: Pope back at work; EU budget stalls; Brazil tied.
beats.body:
Vatican City. Thursday afternoon’s medical update: routine checks were normal, the chest X-ray shows “good recovery of the lung that underwent surgery,” and Pope Leo XIV is doing his daily activities on his own with a full physiotherapy session. He concelebrated Mass again and has resumed work, meeting the Substitute of the Secretariat of State, Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, at Gemelli. Cardinal Parolin said the Nov. 6–17 South America trip will depend on what doctors say after discharge, and that the Pope may reshape parts of his pontificate later if needed; recovery is expected to take about a week in hospital.

Africa. Ethiopian forces and the allied Tigray Peace Force say they have entered Aksum; the monitor ACLED reports Eritrean troops pulling back across the border at Zalambessa, which Eritrea denies. Mauritius police say the island is calm and roads are clear after the week’s unrest.

Asia. A tech selloff hit Asia hardest: South Korea’s KOSPI fell almost 8% and Japan’s Nikkei nearly 5%, though Wall Street ended higher. Japan and the U.S. launched a roughly $21 billion chip-production project in New York state, and Japan’s foreign minister condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Europe. The EU summit ended its first day with no budget breakthrough; Sweden’s Kristersson said a deal may not come even by year’s end. Council President Costa takes over the talks, with a new proposal in a few weeks and a special summit Nov. 26.

North America. U.S. producer prices jumped the most in four and a half years in September, while retail sales beat forecasts; the 10-year Treasury yield had its biggest one-day drop in over a year, to about 5.06%. Tropical Storm Simon weakened to 50 mph off Mexico and should fade by the weekend, with no watches posted.

South America. Datafolha’s runoff poll also shows a tie: Flávio Bolsonaro 51%, Lula 49% of valid votes, within the margin of error, ten days before the Oct. 25 vote.

Oceania. Australia edged New Zealand 24–22 to open the Rugby League World Cup. Fiji’s cabinet endorsed a feasibility study for a roughly US$396 million ship-repair and shipbuilding yard at Lautoka, with Australian support for the next phase.

beats.title: MAGA / MAHA promises kept
beats.headline: Third-country deportations top 16,000; Kennedy vows to end measles outbreak.
beats.body:
“Largest deportation operation in American history.” Promise: Trump pledged mass deportations. What was done: an Al Jazeera analysis of Homeland Security data (via the Berkeley/UCLA Deportation Data Project) counts more than 16,000 third-country deportations, people sent to countries they aren’t from, between January 2025 and August 2026; rights groups put it above 25,000. The Supreme Court allowed the practice to continue in September. Impact: deals with countries like Liberia and Cameroon trade U.S. aid for taking deportees; the UN and rights groups say it risks sending people to danger.

MAHA and measles. Kennedy said Thursday he is “confident I will bring [Pennsylvania’s] outbreak to a quick close,” blaming pandemic-era missed shots. The CDC counts 4,080 U.S. cases this year, the worst since 1991; Pennsylvania has 1,222 cases and five deaths, all unvaccinated, and the CDC sent an investigator this week.

beats.title: World
beats.headline: Vatican City: Pope’s good second night; Yalu bridge opens; EU summit.
beats.body:
Vatican City. The Holy See Press Office said Thursday morning that Pope Leo XIV “had a good night in the hospital, got up and had breakfast”—his second night at Gemelli after Tuesday’s removal of the lower lobe of his right lung. Spokesman Matteo Bruni says the Pope wants to make the Nov. 6–17 Uruguay–Argentina–Peru trip; Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori said recovery could take weeks and the schedule might change, but the Holy See has announced no change. Today’s Bollettino: Father Ignatius Ding Zuyao was ordained bishop of Haimen, China, under the Holy See–China Provisional Agreement, and Bishop Paolo Andreolli, S.X., was named to Ponta de Pedras, Brazil (see Catholic). At the UN, Archbishop El Kassis told the First Committee that disarmament “cannot be postponed until more favourable circumstances arise.”

Africa. Secretary of State Rubio phoned Ethiopia’s Abiy Ahmed urging de-escalation with Eritrea under their 2018 peace deal, as Ethiopian forces expand control in northern Tigray. Kenya confirmed a second Ebola (Bundibugyo) case—a relative of the first patient who was already in quarantine; officials see no community spread. Mauritius extended its curfew through Friday morning after protests over water shortages and living costs; 94 arrests so far (16 minors), and schools are closed Thursday and Friday.

Asia. China and North Korea opened the New Yalu River Bridge Thursday morning—the four-lane, 3-km Dandong–Sinuiju crossing finished in 2014 but idle until now; Premier Li Qiang called it a “new landmark” of friendship. Singapore’s haze peaked at a season-high 24-hour PSI of 212 in the west at noon local time; masks are being distributed and 300+ community centers are serving as haze shelters. The EU–Gulf summit planned for Oct. 24 in Riyadh was postponed after repeated Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s airport.

Europe. EU leaders opened a two-day Brussels summit focused on energy prices (oil above $100, gas at its highest since winter 2022), a sharply divided 2028–34 budget, and Ukraine; draft conclusions lament the U.S. pause on Russian-diesel sanctions, which Bulgaria’s Radev backed as fuel-price relief while most leaders criticized it. Zelenskyy joins Friday. Radev also said he summoned Russia’s ambassador over the Black Sea drone strikes—logic points to Russia, he said, but there is no solid evidence yet; a full terror investigation starts when the ship damaged Tuesday reaches port.

North America. Simon is now a tropical storm (60 mph), nearly stationary about 270 miles south-southeast of Cabo San Lucas; it should drift northwest from Friday and fade by late weekend, with 1–3 inches of rain possible in Baja California Sur and no watches posted. Carney headlines a “Forever Canadian” rally in Calgary tonight ahead of Monday’s Alberta referendum. Panama reported its first death from the Oct. 9 magnitude-7.7 quake, and aftershocks are keeping hundreds from going home.

South America. Brazil’s first Quaest runoff poll has Flávio Bolsonaro 46%, Lula 44%—a statistical tie—ahead of the Oct. 25 vote; Datafolha publishes today. In Colombia, thousands marched peacefully Wednesday, led by ex-president Petro, against President Abelardo de la Espriella’s labor and pension proposals—the opposition’s first big show since he took office in August.

Oceania. Pacific Islands Forum chair Surangel Whipps of Palau, visiting Canberra, pushed back on critics counting absent leaders at last week’s Fiji–Tuvalu pre-COP and pressed for climate finance before COP31 opens Nov. 9; pledges to the Pacific Resilience Facility reached only half of a $500 million goal. Fiji approved a six-month, New Zealand–funded NZSIS review of its intelligence system amid foreign-interference concerns.

beats.title: MAGA / MAHA promises kept
beats.headline: Lower-prices pledge mostly unmet; ACA duplicate-subsidy sweep, some reinstated.
beats.body:
“Your groceries will be cheaper” — cost of living. Promise: Trump vowed cheaper groceries, gas under $2, 2% mortgages, and electricity bills cut in half. What was done: CBS News’s Oct. 14 tally finds food at home up 4% since November 2024, gas at $4.37 (up 47% since the Iran war began in late February), 30-year mortgages at 7.28%, and residential electricity up 12.5% since December 2024. The clear kept item: prescription-drug prices are down 3.9% since their February 2025 peak—the White House credits “most favored nation” pricing; experts also cite GLP-1 competition and more generics. Impact: With September CPI at 3.7%, nine in ten Americans tell CBS prices drive their view of the economy; the White House points to tax cuts, jobs, and trade deals.

“Crush fraud, waste, and abuse” — ACA subsidies. Promise: Kennedy and CMS’s Dr. Oz pledged to stop taxpayer money going where it shouldn’t. What was done: HHS said Oct. 14 it ended Obamacare subsidies this year for 189,000 enrollees who also had Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP or had died, projecting about $1.5 billion in savings over the next year, with a 30-day window to dispute. Impact: KFF Health News (via NPR) reports a separate sweep removed 760,000 enrollees and insurers say CMS has reinstated a small number wrongly cut; 419,000 more sign-ups are under review, with results due after the midterms. Supporters call the cleanup overdue; policy experts say there’s too little data to know how many legitimate members were caught.

SpaceX — Starshield and Starship. Ukraine said new speed limits on moving Starlink/Starshield terminals disrupted drone and interceptor missions; Musk replied that Starshield is “owned and controlled by the U.S. government” and limits are set by the military “and ultimately POTUS.” Ukraine’s Fedorov said Thursday that service at up to 160 km/h is back. Station. Cargo Dragon CRS-35 docks autonomously to Harmony’s space-facing port around 11 a.m. ET (NASA+ coverage from 9:15 a.m.) and stays about a month. The Crew-12 astronauts, home since Oct. 8, brief reporters at 3:30 p.m. ET. NASA also set U.S. spacewalks 100 and 101 for Oct. 29 and Nov. 5: Anil Menon and Canada’s Joshua Kutryk will install the seventh and eighth roll-out solar arrays, raising station power up to 30% (about 160 to 215 kilowatts); preview briefing Tuesday, Oct. 20.

People and the Moon. Artemis II’s Christina Koch becomes NASA’s acting deputy chief engineer Nov. 1 and will no longer be eligible to fly—so all four Artemis II crew members have now moved to other roles. Administrator Isaacman leads an Artemis update Friday, Oct. 23, at 2 p.m. ET at Kennedy on next year’s Artemis III Earth-orbit test and the 2028 landing goal.

Miami. In a new Florida Catholic feature, Archbishop Wenski urges compassion for people with mental illness: “Catholics do not think mental illness should be solved by prayer rather than by psychiatry. We are a people of both.” Catholic Charities (95 this year) offers bilingual, sliding-scale counseling and addiction treatment at St. Luke’s Center. Rome. From Gemelli, Pope Leo sent a message closing the Amoris Laetitia 10th-anniversary meeting: “I ask you please to pray for me, as I pray for you.”

Appointments (Bollettino, Oct. 15). Ponta de Pedras, Brazil: Bishop Paolo Andreolli, S.X.—an Italian-born Xaverian missionary in Pará since 2007 and Belém auxiliary since 2023—becomes diocesan bishop. Haimen, China: Bishop Ignatius Ding Zuyao, 40, appointed Aug. 24 under the Provisional Agreement and pastor in Nantong since 2023, was ordained today. Romania: Greek-Catholic Major Archbishop Claudiu-Lucian Pop united the Eparchy of Cluj-Gherla with the Archeparchy of Făgăraș and Alba Iulia under one bishop.

United States. The USCCB and National Association of Evangelicals issued a joint call for humane, targeted enforcement, keeping families together, due process, and legal pathways. Latin America. Ponta de Pedras above; Peru’s president hopes the November papal visit goes ahead. Europe. The Romanian union above. Africa. Dar es Salaam’s Archbishop Ruwa’ichi invited testimony, favorable or not, for the beatification cause of Tanzania’s founding president Julius Nyerere. Middle East. Lebanon’s ambassador to the Holy See detailed the Pope’s new scholarships for vulnerable Christian families in Lebanon, Syria, and Iraq, run by the Dicastery for the Eastern Churches. Asia. Digital ID, soberly. Six Dutch firms (including ABN AMRO, Rabobank, and KPN) launched “MyCheck,” an EU-compliant digital-identity wallet they’re offering the government free; every EU state must have a digital-ID system by the end of 2026, and Germany’s wallet launches Jan. 2, 2027. It’s voluntary, real infrastructure news—no chips involved.
